Must Know
Use the fastest discriminator first.
Most organism questions can be narrowed by morphology, oxygen requirement, one key biochemical test, and one classic clinical association.
Do not memorize isolated disease lists without the identification pattern.
APPLICATION EDITION

What changed in this version

Case-based focus

Tests now show the result

Biochemical workups are written as test → organism result → how to use it. High-yield examples include TSI, IMViC, MacConkey/EMB, string test, oxidase, CAMP, BBE, Nagler, CCFA, and acid-fast methods.

Toxins are mechanism-first

Major toxins and virulence factors now show the sequence from molecular action → tissue effect → symptom pattern, because mechanism questions are common in application quizzes.

New disease differential tab

Start with pneumonia, meningitis, UTI, diarrhea, wounds, endocarditis, STI, or paralysis, then compare bacteria side-by-side using host clues, symptoms, and decisive tests.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Staphylococcus aureus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → gram-positive cocci, usually in clusters.
    • A clustered GPC result puts Staphylococcus high on the differential.
  • Catalase → positive.
    • Hydrogen peroxide produces foam/bubbles. This separates Staphylococcus from catalase-negative Streptococcus and Enterococcus.
  • Coagulase → positive.
    • Plasma fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, producing visible clotting/clumping. This separates S. aureus from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.
  • Blood agar → golden-yellow colonies. The Basic Bacteriology comparison also shows S. aureus as beta-hemolytic.
    • Use colony appearance only as a clue. Confirm with catalase and coagulase.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Protein A
    • Binds the Fc portion of IgG. This prevents normal orientation for opsonization and helps S. aureus evade phagocytosis.
  • Coagulase
    • Converts fibrinogen → fibrin, coating/clumping bacteria in fibrin.
  • TSST-1
    • Produced at the infection site → enters bloodstream → binds MHC class II as a superantigen → massive cytokine release → fever, rash, hypotension, poor organ perfusion.
  • Panton-Valentine leukocidin
    • Phage encoded → forms pores in WBC membranes → increased cation permeability → release of inflammatory mediators such as IL-8, leukotrienes, and histamine → necrosis and severe inflammation.
  • Hemolysins
    • Alpha targets eukaryotic membranes. Beta degrades sphingomyelin and is RBC-toxic. Delta disrupts membranes. Gamma/leukocidin lyses WBCs.
  • Exfoliative toxins A/B
    • Dissolve the epidermal mucopolysaccharide matrix → generalized desquamation / staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
  • Enterotoxins
    • Heat-stable and resistant to gut enzymes → preformed-toxin food poisoning with short 1–8 h incubation, violent nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, rapid recovery, and usually no fever.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Skin/soft tissue
    • Pimple → furuncle → carbuncle, impetigo, cellulitis, abscess.
  • Disseminated infection
    • Pyomyositis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, bacteremia, septic thrombophlebitis, pneumonia, endocarditis.
  • Toxic shock
    • Abrupt high fever, vomiting/diarrhea, myalgias, sunburn/scarlatiniform rash, hypotension, poor organ perfusion.
  • Food poisoning
    • 1–8 h incubation, violent nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, rapid recovery, typically no fever.
  • Scalded skin syndrome
    • Generalized desquamation from exfoliative toxin.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Culture from surface swab, pus or abscess aspirate, blood, respiratory sample, or CSF as indicated
  • Gram stain shows clustered GPC but cannot alone separate S. aureus from other staphylococci
  • Confirm with catalase → coagulase and susceptibility testing
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Drain closed abscesses and suppurative lesions
  • Use susceptibility testing because resistance is common
  • Lecture MRSA anchors: clindamycin or vancomycin
  • Alternatives listed include tetracycline, TMP-SMX, linezolid, tigecycline, daptomycin, and quinupristin-dalfopristin
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Clustered GPC + catalase positive + coagulase positive. Then decide whether the case is abscess/invasive disease or a toxin syndrome.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Staphylococcus epidermidis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Catalase → positive.
    • Supports Staphylococcus.
  • Coagulase → negative.
    • Places it among coagulase-negative staphylococci.
  • Novobiocin → sensitive.
    • This is the decisive lecture discriminator from S. saprophyticus, which is resistant.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Major high-yield feature is biofilm on prosthetic material
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci are normal skin and mucosal microbiota
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Implanted-device infections involving prostheses, shunts, and catheters
  • Important in very young, elderly, and immunocompromised patients
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Differentiate from S. aureus by coagulase negativity
  • Differentiate from S. saprophyticus by novobiocin sensitivity
  • Interpret cultures with device and clinical context because it is normal skin flora
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture emphasizes that biofilm-associated infections can be difficult to cure and frequently drug-resistant
  • Management is guided by antimicrobial susceptibility and the infected device context
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Coagulase-negative staph + prosthetic material/device + novobiocin sensitive.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Staphylococcus saprophyticus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Catalase → positive.
    • Supports Staphylococcus.
  • Coagulase → negative.
    • Places it among coagulase-negative staphylococci.
  • Novobiocin → resistant.
    • This distinguishes it from S. epidermidis. Pair the result with a UTI in a young woman.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Lecture emphasizes species identification rather than a dedicated toxin profile
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Classic association: urinary tract infection in young women
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococcus followed by novobiocin testing
  • Novobiocin resistance separates it from S. epidermidis
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Use culture and susceptibility results for clinically significant infection
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Young woman with UTI + coagulase-negative staph + novobiocin resistant.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Streptococcus pneumoniae

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Catalase → negative.
    • Supports Streptococcus rather than Staphylococcus.
  • Blood agar → alpha hemolysis.
    • Partial hemoglobin breakdown produces the greenish alpha-hemolytic pattern described in the lecture.
  • Optochin → sensitive.
    • Fast discriminator from viridans streptococci, which are optochin resistant.
  • Bile solubility → soluble.
    • Viridans streptococci are bile insoluble.
  • Morphology → encapsulated, lancet-shaped diplococci or short chains.
    • In a case with asplenia plus pneumonia or meningitis, this combination is especially high yield.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Polysaccharide capsule
    • Prevents efficient phagocytosis. Risk rises in anatomic or functional asplenia because opsonized encapsulated organisms are cleared poorly.
  • IgA protease
    • Cleaves mucosal IgA → weakens the first-line mucosal antibody barrier → facilitates otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, and meningitis.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Pneumonia
    • Classic lecture clue: rust-colored sputum.
  • MOPS pattern
    • Meningitis, otitis media, pneumonia, sinusitis.
  • Asplenia clue
    • Fever, malaise, rapidly progressive sepsis in an anatomic/functional asplenic patient should raise concern for an encapsulated organism such as pneumococcus.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Alpha-hemolytic streptococcus → optochin testing and bile solubility
  • Lecture differentiation: pneumococcus is optochin sensitive while viridans is resistant
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Use susceptibility-guided therapy for invasive disease
  • Lecture prevention emphasis includes pneumococcal vaccination in high-risk patients
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble encapsulated diplococcus + rust sputum or meningitis, especially with asplenia.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Viridans streptococci

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Catalase → negative.
    • Supports Streptococcus.
  • Blood agar → alpha hemolysis.
    • Shares this result with S. pneumoniae.
  • Optochin → resistant.
    • Separates viridans from optochin-sensitive S. pneumoniae.
  • Bile solubility → insoluble.
    • Opposite the pneumococcal result.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Biofilm / oral adhesion
    • Promotes attachment in the oral cavity. The lecture connects members such as S. mutans and S. mitis with oral biofilm and gingival disease.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Subacute infective endocarditis
  • Dental and oral associations including caries for members such as S. mutans
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Alpha hemolysis followed by optochin resistance distinguishes viridans from S. pneumoniae
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture management is syndrome-directed, especially for infective endocarditis
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, bile-insoluble oral streptococcus + dental disease or subacute endocarditis.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus)

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Blood agar → beta hemolysis.
    • Complete hemolysis places the isolate among beta-hemolytic streptococci.
  • Bacitracin → sensitive.
    • Separates GAS from bacitracin-resistant GBS in the lecture.
  • PYR → positive.
    • Supports S. pyogenes.
  • Lancefield antigen → Group A.
    • Cell-wall carbohydrate grouping confirms the GAS identity.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • M protein
    • Major virulence factor that inhibits C3b-mediated opsonization. It also shares structural similarity with cardiac myosin → molecular mimicry → cross-reactive antibodies/T cells → acute rheumatic fever.
  • Streptococcal pyrogenic/erythrogenic toxins
    • The lecture links toxin-mediated disease to scarlet-fever type findings and toxin-driven invasive syndromes.
  • Streptolysins
    • Toxin/enzyme set contributes to tissue injury and beta hemolysis.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Pharyngitis and tonsillitis
  • Scarlet fever and skin infections
  • Erysipelas and invasive streptococcal disease
  • Post-infectious rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis are key exam associations
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Beta-hemolytic streptococcus → bacitracin and PYR pattern
  • Throat culture or other syndrome-appropriate specimen
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture: penicillin is the main treatment anchor
  • Macrolide is listed when allergic to penicillin
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Beta-hemolytic + bacitracin-sensitive + PYR-positive Group A strep + pharyngitis/skin disease or post-strep immune sequelae.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Blood agar → beta hemolysis.
    • Shares beta hemolysis with S. pyogenes.
  • Bacitracin → resistant.
    • Opposite the GAS result.
  • PYR → negative and hippurate → positive.
    • The lecture mnemonic links these results to Group B strep.
  • CAMP → positive.
    • CAMP enlarges the area of hemolysis produced beside S. aureus.
  • Pregnancy screening → vaginal + rectal swab at 35–37 weeks.
    • A positive screen leads to intrapartum penicillin in the lecture.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule
    • Antiphagocytic virulence factor supporting invasive neonatal disease.
  • CAMP factor
    • Primarily a laboratory identification clue in this lecture. It enlarges the zone of S. aureus hemolysis.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis
  • Maternal colonization is the high-yield obstetric setting
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Pregnancy screening with vaginal and rectal swabs at 35–37 weeks
  • CAMP and hippurate tests help distinguish it from GAS
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • If maternal screen is positive → intrapartum penicillin
  • Lecture drug of choice: Penicillin G
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Neonate with sepsis/pneumonia/meningitis or positive maternal 35–37-week screen + CAMP/hippurate positive.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → gram-negative diplococci, often intracellular in PMNs.
    • Coffee-bean-like diplococci plus neutrophils support gonococcus in the right syndrome.
  • Oxidase → positive and catalase → positive.
    • Supports Neisseria.
  • Carbohydrate use → glucose only.
    • This separates gonococcus from N. meningitidis, which uses glucose + maltose.
  • Selective culture → Thayer-Martin/VCN when culture is required.
    • NAAT is a major diagnostic method in the lecture.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Pili
    • Mediate mucosal attachment and undergo antigenic variation → immune escape and lack of durable protective immunity.
  • IgA protease
    • Destroys mucosal IgA → weakens mucosal defense.
  • Catalase
    • Breaks down hydrogen peroxide inside neutrophil phagosomes → helps survival after phagocytosis.
  • LOS
    • Acts as endotoxin and contributes to inflammatory tissue injury and disseminated disease.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Urethritis and cervicitis
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Ophthalmia neonatorum
  • Disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis and skin findings
  • Gonococcal endocarditis can occur
Diagnostic confirmation
  • NAAT is an important diagnostic method
  • Culture on selective media is used when needed, including susceptibility workup
  • Gram stain is useful especially in symptomatic male urethritis
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture first-line anchor: third-generation cephalosporin
  • The lecture regimen lists ceftriaxone and coverage for possible Chlamydia coinfection
  • Prevention includes safer sex, partner evaluation and neonatal eye prophylaxis
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Intracellular GND + oxidase positive + glucose only + urethritis/cervicitis/PID or disseminated arthritis.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Neisseria meningitidis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → gram-negative diplococci.
    • Interpret with CSF/blood and the meningitis or meningococcemia syndrome.
  • Oxidase → positive and catalase → positive.
    • Supports Neisseria.
  • Carbohydrate use → glucose + maltose.
    • Decisive lecture discriminator from gonococcus.
  • Capsule → present.
    • A major invasive-disease clue and another difference from N. gonorrhoeae.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule
    • Antiphagocytic and central to invasive bloodstream/CNS disease.
  • LOS endotoxin
    • Massive systemic inflammatory activation → vascular injury, shock, purpura/DIC, and fulminant meningococcemia.
  • IgA protease + pili/Opa
    • Support nasopharyngeal colonization and adherence before invasion.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Meningococcal meningitis
  • Meningococcemia with petechiae or purpura
  • Fulminant disease with shock and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  • Complement C5–C9 deficiency and asplenia are major risk clues
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Blood and CSF are key specimens
  • Gram stain and culture, plus syndrome-appropriate rapid methods
  • Differentiate from gonococcus by maltose fermentation and capsule
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment uses a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone
  • Prevention includes vaccination and management of close contacts
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Meningitis or purpuric shock + GND + capsule + glucose and maltose.

SALMONELLA VS SHIGELLA

The comparison that wins exam points

Lecture p. 4–7
FeatureSalmonellaShigella
LactoseNon-lactose fermenterNon-lactose fermenter. S. sonnei may ferment lactose slowly.
MotilityMotileNon-motile
H₂SPositive in classic differentiationNegative
Major antigen clueTyphi has Vi capsular antigenNo H antigen and no K antigen

KLEBSIELLA / PROTEUS / CITROBACTER

Three high-yield opportunists

Lecture p. 8–12

Klebsiella

Lactose fermenter with a prominent capsule and non-motile pattern. Lecture emphasizes pneumonia and UTI, plus the protective capsule as a major virulence factor.

Proteus

Swarming motility and strong urease pattern. Lecture links urease to urinary infection and stone formation. Proteus lacks K antigen.

Citrobacter

Grouped with lactose fermenters, though some species produce H₂S. Lecture emphasizes opportunistic infection and neonatal CNS disease patterns.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Escherichia coli

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • MacConkey → lactose fermenter.
    • Produces pink colonies.
  • EMB → metallic green sheen.
    • A classic E. coli culture clue in the lecture.
  • SMAC for O157:H7 → colorless/pale colonies.
    • Regular E. coli turns pink while O157:H7 is highlighted as the dangerous non-sorbitol pattern in the lecture.
  • TSI → A/A + gas, no H₂S.
    • Both slant and butt are acid. Gas is produced. No black H₂S reaction.
  • IMViC → ++--.
    • Indole +, methyl red +, VP −, citrate −.
  • Motility → positive, urease → negative, oxidase → negative, catalase → positive.
    • This biochemical cluster helps separate E. coli from Klebsiella and Proteus.
  • Diarrheagenic molecular workup.
    • EHEC/STEC PCR detects stx1/stx2. ETEC PCR detects lt/st. EPEC PCR detects eae. ELISA can detect Shiga toxins in stool.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • LPS / O antigen
    • Endotoxin spill during bacteremia → intense cytokine response and septic shock.
  • ETEC LT + ST enterotoxins
    • Drive intestinal cells to secrete large amounts of water and salt → acute watery traveler’s diarrhea. The lecture identifies lt and st genes by PCR.
  • EHEC Shiga toxin
    • Shuts down host protein production → colonic hemorrhage → bloody diarrhea. Systemic toxin effect is linked to acute renal failure / hemolytic uremic syndrome.
  • Type III secretion + intimin
    • For EPEC/EHEC, bacterial proteins alter actin and create attaching-and-effacing lesions → reduced water absorption and diarrhea.
  • P fimbriae / Type 1 pili
    • Anchor urinary strains despite urine flow → UTI and ascending infection.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • ETEC → traveler’s watery diarrhea
  • EPEC → infantile diarrhea
  • EHEC → bloody diarrhea and HUS
  • UPEC → cystitis and pyelonephritis
  • Urosepsis and bacteremia
  • Neonatal meningitis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Urine, stool, or blood according to syndrome
  • SMAC helps identify O157:H7 as pale or colorless
  • Lecture highlights latex agglutination, Shiga-toxin ELISA, and PCR for diarrheagenic strains
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Management depends on syndrome and susceptibility
  • For diarrheal disease, assess dehydration and complications
  • Avoid treating outside the lecture-specific framework when the strain and syndrome have not been identified
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Lactose-positive enteric + EMB metallic sheen + indole positive. Then use syndrome to choose UPEC vs diarrheagenic pathotype.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Salmonella

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • MacConkey → non-lactose fermenter.
    • Colorless colonies.
  • SS / HE / XLD → colonies with black centers when H₂S is produced.
    • SS: colorless with black centers. HE: blue-green with black centers. XLD: red with black centers.
  • TSI → K/A + gas + H₂S.
    • Red/alkaline slant with yellow/acid butt. Blackening indicates H₂S.
  • Motility → positive, urease → negative, indole → negative.
    • Motility + H₂S are fast ways to separate Salmonella from Shigella.
  • Specimen choice.
    • Stool for gastroenteritis. Blood is emphasized for typhoid. Urine and bone marrow may also be used.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Invasion + intracellular survival
    • Intestinal invasion and macrophage transport are central. The lecture describes inflammasome/caspase-1 activation and pyroptosis with IL-1β and IL-18 in pathogenesis.
  • Vi capsule of S. Typhi
    • Capsular antigen supports immune evasion and systemic enteric fever.
  • LPS
    • Endotoxin contributes to systemic inflammation in bacteremia.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Gastroenteritis
  • Enteric or typhoid fever
  • Bacteremia and systemic disease are high-yield complications
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Stool culture for gastroenteritis
  • Blood culture for typhoid
  • Urine and bone marrow can also be used in enteric fever workup
  • Differentiate from Shigella by motility and H₂S production
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment varies with enteric fever versus uncomplicated gastroenteritis and antimicrobial susceptibility
  • Prevention emphasizes food, water, and sanitation measures
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Non-lactose fermenter + motile + H₂S blackening. Typhoid cases prioritize blood culture.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Shigella

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • MacConkey → usually non-lactose fermenting.
    • Colorless colonies. S. sonnei may ferment lactose slowly.
  • SS / XLD → no black centers.
    • Absent H₂S helps separate Shigella from Salmonella.
  • TSI → K/A, no gas, no H₂S.
    • Slant red/pink, butt yellow. No gas bubbles and no blackening.
  • Motility → negative and urease → negative.
    • Non-motility is a major exam discriminator.
  • PCR → ipaH.
    • Lecture calls multiplex PCR a modern gold-standard approach. Shiga toxin can also be detected by ELISA or PCR.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Type III secretion
    • After macrophage uptake, injected proteins trigger pyroptosis → macrophage rupture → organisms access the basolateral side of colonic epithelium.
  • IcsA / VirG
    • Hijacks actin polymerization → “rocket-tail” cell-to-cell spread without returning to the extracellular space.
  • Shiga toxin
    • Major toxin association. Protein-synthesis inhibition contributes to mucosal injury and severe systemic complications.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Bacillary dysentery with fever, abdominal cramps, tenesmus, and frequent small-volume bloody mucoid stools
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Fresh stool, especially blood, mucus, or pus portion
  • Culture on enteric selective media
  • Biochemical profile separates it from Salmonella by nonmotility and absent H₂S
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Support hydration and manage according to severity and susceptibility
  • Prevention focuses on fecal-oral transmission control and sanitation
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Bloody mucoid small-volume stool + tenesmus + nonmotile + no H₂S + K/A no gas.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Klebsiella

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → gram-negative, short, plump straight rods.
    • Capsule can be visualized with India ink in the lecture workup.
  • MacConkey → vigorous lactose fermenter.
    • Large, bright pink-to-red colonies that are heavy, glistening, wet, and mucoid.
  • Blood agar → large dome-shaped grayish-white non-hemolytic, very slimy colonies.
    • The slimy appearance reflects the thick capsule.
  • EMB → large mucoid pink-to-purple colonies without metallic green sheen.
    • This helps separate it from E. coli.
  • String test → positive hypermucoviscosity when thread >5 mm.
    • The lecture associates this with hypervirulent K. pneumoniae.
  • IMViC → --++.
    • Indole −, MR −, VP +, citrate +.
  • Urease → weak-to-moderate positive.
    • Useful with the rest of the biochemical pattern.
  • TSI → A/A + heavy gas, no H₂S.
    • Both slant and butt turn bright yellow. No blackening.
  • Motility → negative.
    • Klebsiella also lacks the H flagellar antigen in the lecture.
  • Resistance workup.
    • AST is important. Multiplex PCR may detect carbapenemase genes such as blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48, blaVIM.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • K polysaccharide capsule
    • Thick slimy capsule blocks macrophage/neutrophil phagocytosis and traps complement away from the cell surface → mucoid colonies and marked virulence.
  • LPS / O antigen
    • Potent endotoxin in the bloodstream → systemic cytokine overreaction → endotoxic septic shock.
  • Siderophores
    • Enterobactin/yersiniabactin draw iron from host storage proteins such as transferrin → supports rapid tissue replication.
  • Type 1 + Type 3 fimbriae
    • Adhere to host surfaces. Type 3 fimbriae promote dense biofilm on urinary catheters and breathing tubes.
  • Important exam point
    • The lecture mnemonic identifies Klebsiella as the Enterobacteriaceae member without exotoxin. Its disease is driven by capsule, endotoxin, adhesins, siderophores, and host inflammatory damage rather than a named exotoxin.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Lobar pneumonia
    • High-risk setting: chronic alcohol use, diabetes, weakened lungs/immune system, hospitalized or ventilated patient.
    • Symptoms: sudden high fever + chills, severe productive cough, currant-jelly sputum, pleurisy, dyspnea, cyanosis.
    • Imaging: lung abscesses and cavitation.
  • UTI
    • Common in hospital settings and urinary-catheter patients.
    • Symptoms: dysuria, urgency, frequency, cloudy alkaline urine, possible pyelonephritis.
  • Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae syndrome
    • Can affect otherwise young/healthy people.
    • Pyogenic liver abscess with metastatic spread to endophthalmitis or meningitis.
  • Sepsis/bacteremia
    • Spread from lung, catheter, or liver abscess → tachycardia, tachypnea, marked lethargy/altered mental state, septic shock, and multiorgan failure.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Sputum, urine, blood, or CSF depending on syndrome
  • Hypermucoviscosity may be assessed with the string test
  • Culture and biochemical pattern are strongly discriminating
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Use antimicrobial susceptibility because resistant hospital strains are important
  • Prevention emphasizes healthcare infection-control measures
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Currant-jelly pneumonia or catheter UTI + very mucoid lactose-positive nonmotile rod + --++ IMViC + weak/moderate urease + string test >5 mm if hypervirulent.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Proteus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Blood agar → swarming motility.
    • Wave-like spreading across the plate is a signature clue.
  • MacConkey → non-lactose fermenter.
    • Colorless colonies.
  • Urease → strongly positive.
    • Urea is hydrolyzed to ammonia. Urine becomes highly alkaline, often pH >7.2 and may reach 8–9 in the lecture mechanism.
  • H₂S → positive and TSI → K/A + H₂S.
    • Blackening supports H₂S production.
  • Phenylalanine deaminase → positive.
    • Listed as a special diagnostic test in the lecture appendix.
  • Indole → P. vulgaris is positive.
    • Species-level discriminator highlighted in the lecture.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Urease
    • Urea → ammonia + carbamate → ammonia binds H+ and raises urine pH to markedly alkaline levels → direct mucosal injury + precipitation of struvite and carbonate-apatite crystals → stone formation.
  • Swarming + fimbriae
    • Hyperflagellated swarm cells move along urinary surfaces. MR/P fimbriae then anchor to bladder/kidney epithelium.
  • Crystalline biofilm
    • Mineral crystals become trapped in biofilm on catheters → obstructive, protected bacterial reservoir.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Urinary tract infection
  • Lecture links urease-driven alkaline urine with urinary stone formation
  • Can be isolated from wounds and bloodstream
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Urine, wound swab, or blood
  • Look for swarming on culture plus strong urease positivity
  • Differentiate species with indole and other biochemical reactions
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Treatment should follow culture and susceptibility results
  • Correct urinary obstruction or stone-related complications when clinically present
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: UTI + strongly alkaline urine/struvite stone + swarming + strong urease + H₂S.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Citrobacter

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • MacConkey.
    • C. freundii is a slow lactose fermenter with smooth pale-pink colonies. C. koseri is non-lactose fermenting and may be colorless/pale.
  • EMB → translucent pinkish-purple colonies, no metallic green sheen.
    • Helps separate from E. coli.
  • XLD / HE → C. freundii may form black-centered colonies from H₂S.
    • H₂S is species-variable.
  • Citrate → positive and ONPG → positive.
    • Lecture calls these a definitive bench check.
  • TSI.
    • C. freundii: A/A or K/A + gas + heavy H₂S. C. koseri: K/A + gas but no H₂S.
  • IMViC.
    • C. freundii: − + − +. C. koseri: + + − +.
  • Motility → positive, urease → variable/weakly positive.
    • Use species-level biochemical pattern rather than one isolated test.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Opportunistic enteric pathogen
  • Lecture emphasizes biochemical variability rather than a single defining exotoxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • UTI, bacteremia, wound infection, and CNS infection depending on species and host
  • Citrobacter koseri is an exam association with neonatal meningitis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Urine, blood, wound, or CSF
  • Culture resembles other enterics so biochemical testing is important
  • H₂S production can help separate some Citrobacter from E. coli
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Use species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
  • Healthcare infection-control measures are important for nosocomial disease
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Opportunistic enteric infection. In a neonate with meningitis/brain abscess think C. koseri and use species-level biochemical pattern.
SPORES

Sporulation and germination

Must Know
Lecture notes that spores are extremely resistant and may remain viable for years.
Autoclave anchor: 120°C for 15 minutes.
In living animals and humans, Bacillus is in the vegetative form rather than the sporulated form.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Bacillus anthracis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Blood agar → irregular fringe-like Medusa head colonies.
    • A classic colony morphology clue.
  • Bicarbonate agar → mucoid colony when capsule is produced.
    • Demonstrates the capsule.
  • Gamma phage → lysis positive.
    • A positive lysis result supports B. anthracis. B. cereus is negative in the lecture comparison.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • D-glutamic acid capsule, pXO2
    • Antiphagocytic.
  • Protective antigen
    • Attachment component that permits toxin entry into host cells.
  • Edema factor
    • Generates/increases intracellular cAMP → edema and impaired neutrophil phagocytic function.
  • Lethal factor
    • Promotes macrophage death and disrupts inflammatory mediators described in the lecture.
  • PA + EF + LF
    • Act synergistically to produce systemic anthrax.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Cutaneous anthrax → painless black eschar or malignant pustule
  • Inhalational anthrax → Woolsorter’s disease with mediastinal lymph-node enlargement and rapid respiratory failure
  • Gastrointestinal anthrax after contaminated food
  • Septicemia can follow local disease
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Specimen depends on syndrome: pustule, sputum, or blood
  • Bicarbonate agar, BAP colony morphology, gamma phage test, and ELISA are lecture anchors
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline with one or two additional antibiotics
  • Lecture additional agents include rifampin, vancomycin, penicillin, and imipenem
  • Prevention includes animal control, sterilization of animal products, and vaccination strategies
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Painless black eschar or inhalational disease + Medusa-head colony + gamma-phage lysis + pXO1/pXO2 virulence.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Bacillus cereus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Spore-forming Bacillus species
  • Lecture food source clues: fried rice, cereals, sauces, and pasta
  • Gamma phage lysis is negative in the B. anthracis comparison
  • Clinical food history plus culture when indicated
  • Distinguish from B. anthracis with morphology and gamma phage response
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Emetic toxin
    • Heat-stable toxin associated with the short-incubation vomiting syndrome, classically after rice/starchy food.
  • Diarrheal toxin
    • Heat-labile enterotoxin associated with the longer-incubation diarrheal syndrome.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Food poisoning or “Chinese Restaurant Syndrome”
  • Emetic syndrome with short incubation after rice or starch food
  • Diarrheal gastroenteritis with longer incubation
  • Can cause severe ophthalmitis after soil-contaminated penetrating eye injury
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Clinical food history plus culture when indicated
  • Distinguish from B. anthracis with morphology and gamma phage response
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • GI disease is commonly self-limited in the lecture
  • Ophthalmitis treatment listed: vancomycin, clindamycin, gentamicin
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Food poisoning or “Chinese Restaurant Syndrome” Emetic syndrome with short incubation after rice or starch food
ORGANISM PROFILE

Bacillus thuringiensis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Spore-forming Bacillus discussed as a minor related species
  • No dedicated human diagnostic workup is emphasized
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Produces a plasmid-associated protein lethal to insect larvae
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Lecture emphasis is agricultural and larvicidal use rather than a human disease syndrome
Diagnostic confirmation
  • No dedicated human diagnostic workup is emphasized
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • No dedicated human treatment is emphasized in this lecture
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Lecture emphasis is agricultural and larvicidal use rather than a human disease syndrome
ORGANISM PROFILE

Corynebacterium diphtheriae

Lecture p. 3
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Microscopy → club-shaped rods in Chinese-letter arrangements with metachromatic Babes-Ernst/volutin granules.
    • The granules are a classic morphology clue.
  • Loeffler medium → enhances demonstration of metachromatic granules.
    • Used for characteristic morphology.
  • Tellurite medium → gray-black colonies.
    • Selective/differential culture clue.
  • Elek test → determines toxigenicity.
    • A culture isolate is not enough. The high-yield question is whether the strain produces diphtheria toxin.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Diphtheria toxin
    • Beta-phage encoded A-B toxin. B fragment binds host cell → A fragment enters → ADP-ribosylates/inactivates EF-2 → blocks protein synthesis → local pseudomembrane injury plus systemic myocarditis and neurologic toxicity.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Respiratory diphtheria with adherent pseudomembrane and bull neck
  • Airway obstruction
  • Myocarditis
  • Cranial nerve and skeletal-muscle paralysis
  • Cutaneous diphtheria with deep non-healing ulcer
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Nasopharyngeal or throat swab
  • Loeffler slant, tellurite media, and Elek toxigenicity test
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Diphtheria antitoxin plus penicillin as an adjunct
  • Prevention is toxoid vaccination and management of exposed contacts
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Pseudomembrane/bull neck + club-shaped metachromatic rods. Elek positivity proves toxigenicity.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Listeria monocytogenes

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Catalase → positive.
    • Helps separate Listeria from catalase-negative streptococci when morphology is confusing.
  • Motility → tumbling at 25°C.
    • Classic laboratory clue.
  • Blood agar → narrow beta hemolysis.
    • Use with catalase and motility.
  • Esculin hydrolysis → positive.
    • Additional biochemical clue in the lecture.
  • Cold growth → can grow at refrigerator temperature.
    • Important foodborne recognition clue.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Internalin
    • Promotes entry into host cells.
  • Listeriolysin O + phospholipase
    • Disrupt phagosomal membrane → organism escapes into cytoplasm.
  • ActA
    • Hijacks host actin polymerization → intracellular movement and direct cell-to-cell spread.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Foodborne listeriosis
  • High-risk groups: pregnant patients, newborns, elderly, immunocompromised
  • Pregnancy → bacteremia and fetal loss
  • Neonatal sepsis and meningitis
  • CNS disease in vulnerable hosts
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Culture plus catalase, beta hemolysis, and tumbling motility
  • Cold tolerance is a useful identification clue
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture drug anchors include ampicillin, with vancomycin and ciprofloxacin also listed in its comparison table
  • Prevention centers on food safety in high-risk groups
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Pregnant/newborn/elderly/immunocompromised + meningitis/sepsis + catalase positive + tumbling motility + beta hemolysis.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae

Lecture p. 6
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-positive rods in short chains
  • Catalase negative, oxidase negative, indole negative
  • Produces H₂S
  • BAP with alpha hemolysis under 5–10% CO₂
  • Resistant to smoking, pickling, and desiccation
  • Aspirate or biopsy from lesion margin
  • Gram stain, BAP culture, and H₂S production
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Hyaluronidase hydrolyzes hyaluronic acid
  • Neuraminidase supports adhesion
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Erysipeloid after occupational contact with infected fish or pork
  • Classic clues: “seal finger” and “whale finger”
  • Painful slowly spreading inflammation at traumatized skin
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Aspirate or biopsy from lesion margin
  • Gram stain, BAP culture, and H₂S production
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment comparison lists penicillin
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Erysipeloid after occupational contact with infected fish or pork Classic clues: “seal finger” and “whale finger”
ORGANISM PROFILE

Lactobacilli

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-positive rods
  • Non-spore-forming
  • Non-motile
  • Facultative anaerobes
  • Grow as small white creamy colonies on MRS agar
  • MRS agar and Gram morphology are lecture anchors
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Normal oral, GI, and vaginal flora
  • Ferment available sugars or glycogen to lactic acid, helping maintain an acidic environment
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Lecture emphasizes beneficial normal-flora and probiotic roles rather than a major disease syndrome
Diagnostic confirmation
  • MRS agar and Gram morphology are lecture anchors
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Used commercially as probiotics and in fermented foods
  • No pathogen-specific treatment emphasized
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Lecture emphasizes beneficial normal-flora and probiotic roles rather than a major disease syndrome

Streptomyces species

Lecture p. 6
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-positive aerobic bacteria
  • Chains of spores at maturity
  • Colorful fungus-like colonies
  • No dedicated clinical diagnostic algorithm emphasized
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Lecture focus is environmental metabolism and natural antimicrobial production rather than a human toxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Main lecture emphasis is soil ecology and antibiotic production
Diagnostic confirmation
  • No dedicated clinical diagnostic algorithm emphasized
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Produces many drugs listed in the lecture, including streptomycin, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, neomycin, lincomycin, and others
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Main lecture emphasis is soil ecology and antibiotic production
ORGANISM PROFILE

Nocardia

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Microscopy → branching filamentous Gram-positive rods.
    • Can resemble fungi morphologically.
  • Modified acid-fast stain → weakly acid-fast.
    • This separates it from non-acid-fast Actinomyces in an application stem.
  • Culture → may require prolonged incubation.
    • PCR and histopathology are also lecture anchors.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Filamentous branching growth and intracellular persistence are central exam features
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Pulmonary nocardiosis
  • CNS dissemination including brain abscess
  • Cutaneous disease and mycetoma can occur, especially in immunocompromised hosts
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Microscopy for branching acid-fast bacilli
  • Histopathology may show grains with surrounding neutrophils
  • PCR and culture are lecture anchors
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment anchor: TMP-SMX
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Pulmonary nocardiosis CNS dissemination including brain abscess
ORGANISM PROFILE

Campylobacter jejuni

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-negative curved or spiral bacillus
  • Highly motile with polar flagella
  • Microaerophilic
  • Lecture identifies oxidase and catalase positivity and growth characteristics used in pathogen identification
  • Stool-based microbiologic workup
  • Curved morphology, microaerophilic growth, and enzymatic profile are key identification clues
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Motility helps movement through mucus
  • Lecture focuses on foodborne intestinal invasion rather than one named exotoxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Gastroenteritis and traveler’s diarrhea
  • Major source clue: undercooked or contaminated chicken
  • Can be severe in very young, elderly, or immunocompromised patients
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Stool-based microbiologic workup
  • Curved morphology, microaerophilic growth, and enzymatic profile are key identification clues
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Supportive care is central for uncomplicated gastroenteritis
  • Antimicrobial treatment is reserved according to severity and lecture guidance
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Gastroenteritis and traveler’s diarrhea Major source clue: undercooked or contaminated chicken
ORGANISM PROFILE

Helicobacter pylori

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Urease → positive.
    • Urea → ammonia + CO₂. The ammonia helps neutralize the acidic gastric environment.
  • Oxidase → positive and catalase → positive.
    • Together with urease, the lecture calls this the triple-positive enzymatic signature.
  • Rapid urease test → detects urease activity from biopsy.
    • Invasive test.
  • Urea breath test → highly specific for active infection.
    • Preferred in the lecture for confirming eradication.
  • Stool antigen → detects active infection.
    • Also used to confirm eradication.
  • Serology IgG → antibodies.
    • Limitation: cannot distinguish active from past eradicated infection.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Urease
    • Urea → ammonia + CO₂ → locally buffers gastric acid and permits colonization.
  • Flagella
    • Propel the organism through gastric mucus.
  • BabA adhesin
    • Anchors the organism to gastric epithelium.
  • VacA
    • Induces severe epithelial vacuole formation → cell injury/death.
  • CagA
    • Alters host-cell signaling → intense inflammation → markedly increased gastric-carcinoma risk in the lecture.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Chronic gastritis
  • Peptic and duodenal ulcer disease
  • GI bleeding risk
  • Lecture identifies H. pylori as a Class I carcinogen and major gastric-cancer risk factor
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Invasive: rapid urease test, histology, culture, PCR
  • Non-invasive: urea breath test, stool antigen, serology
  • Serology cannot distinguish active from past cleared infection
  • Urea breath or stool antigen is used to confirm eradication
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture: 14-day combination of two antibiotics such as amoxicillin and clarithromycin plus a PPI
  • Confirm eradication after 4 weeks with urea breath or stool antigen
  • No licensed vaccine
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Gastritis/ulcer + urease/oxidase/catalase triple positive. Use urea breath or stool antigen for active infection/eradication.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Vibrio cholerae

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • TCBS → sucrose fermentation turns the medium yellow.
    • Key culture discriminator from V. parahaemolyticus.
  • Oxidase → positive.
    • Supports Vibrio.
  • Stool culture / serogrouping.
    • O1 and O139 are emphasized as epidemic strains.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Cholera toxin A-B
    • B subunit binds host cell. A1 is the toxic component, linked through A2 → increases intracellular cAMP → chloride/electrolyte secretion → massive water loss → rice-water diarrhea and dehydration.
  • TCP
    • Toxin-coregulated pilus is a colonization factor and receptor for CTX phage.
  • Mucinase
    • Helps penetrate the small-intestinal mucus layer.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Cholera with profuse watery or “rice-water” stool and rapid dehydration
  • Tachycardia, hypotension, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucosa, thirst, and cramps are dehydration clues
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Stool culture on TCBS and serogroup differentiation
  • Lecture also discusses phage and polymyxin-B differentiation
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Aggressive rehydration is the primary treatment
  • Antibiotics are added as indicated
  • Prevention: sanitation, safe drinking water, and disinfection of stool and vomitus
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Profuse rice-water diarrhea + severe dehydration + TCBS yellow + cholera toxin cAMP mechanism.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • TCBS → no sucrose fermentation, so there is no yellow change.
    • Opposite V. cholerae.
  • Wagatsuma agar → hemolysis from TDH.
    • The lecture links this to the Kanagawa phenomenon.
  • Urease → listed as a virulence-associated biochemical feature.
    • Pair the laboratory result with seafood/water exposure.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • TDH / TRH hemolysins
    • Thermostable direct hemolysin and related hemolysin damage membranes. The lecture links TDH hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar to the Kanagawa phenomenon and “meat-wash” watery stool.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Foodborne seafood-associated gastroenteritis
  • Cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills
  • Can cause septicemia
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Wagatsuma agar for hemolysin activity
  • TCBS differentiation from V. cholerae
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • In immunocompetent patients the lecture describes gastroenteritis as usually self-limited
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Foodborne seafood-associated gastroenteritis Cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills
ORGANISM PROFILE

Vibrio vulnificus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Oxidase-positive fermenter
  • Lactose positive and capsulated
  • Halophilic
  • Naturally present in coastal and estuarine waters
  • Culture from blood or wound according to syndrome plus Vibrio biochemical identification
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule and invasive potential are the dominant lecture clues
  • Lecture calls it the most virulent non-cholera Vibrio
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Diarrhea and abdominal pain after raw or undercooked seafood
  • Wound infection after seawater exposure
  • Cellulitis and severe soft-tissue disease
  • Septicemia especially in patients with liver disease
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Culture from blood or wound according to syndrome plus Vibrio biochemical identification
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Rapid recognition and treatment are critical for septicemia or necrotizing soft-tissue disease
  • Lecture does not provide a dedicated drug table for this species

ORGANISM PROFILE

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • MacConkey → non-lactose fermenter.
    • No pink lactose-fermenting colony pattern.
  • Isolation agar / colony pigment → pyocyanin blue-green.
    • Water-soluble pigment is a strong visual clue.
  • Oxidase → positive.
    • Tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine is converted to indophenols in the lecture demonstration.
  • Temperature → can grow at 42°C.
    • Useful against Acinetobacter baumannii, which the lecture notes can grow at 44°C.
  • UV → fluorescence.
    • Related to fluorescent pigment production.
  • Other case clues → fruity odor, blue-green pigment.
    • Pair these with burn wounds, CF, ventilators, hot tubs, swimmer’s ear, or catheters.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Slime layer / biofilm
    • Promotes attachment, blocks phagocytosis, and limits antibiotic penetration. In respiratory disease it weakens ciliary clearance.
  • LPS
    • Endotoxin → fever, shock, oliguria, and DIC.
  • Exotoxin A
    • Blocks host protein synthesis.
  • Exoenzyme S
    • Adhesive/toxic factor emphasized in burned tissue and respiratory-cell interaction.
  • Phospholipase C
    • Attacks pulmonary cells → atelectasis and necrosis.
  • Alkaline protease
    • Lyses fibrin → hemorrhagic skin lesions and corneal infection.
  • Elastase
    • Breaks elastic fibers in alveoli, interferes with cilia, and degrades IgG, IgA, complement, collagen, and coagulation factors.
  • Pyochelin
    • Siderophore produced when iron is low → scavenges iron for bacterial use.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Host settings
    • Respiratory equipment, cystic fibrosis, injection-drug use/contaminated needles, immunocompromise, severe burns.
  • Ear
    • External otitis/swimmer’s ear with greenish discharge after contaminated-water exposure and maceration.
  • Blood/skin
    • Bacteremia can produce ecthyma gangrenosum, including in severely burned patients.
  • Water exposure
    • Hot-tub folliculitis after inadequately chlorinated pools/spas.
  • Urinary
    • Catheters, instruments, irrigating solutions can introduce the organism.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Blood agar, MacConkey, and isolation agar
  • Oxidase positive, 42°C growth, pigments, and fruity odor are classic clues
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture lists susceptibility to aminoglycosides such as amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin
  • Resistance is promoted by biofilm and R-factor plasmids, so susceptibility testing is important
  • Contact precautions are emphasized for MDR strains
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Burn/CF/VAP/hot tub/swimmer’s ear + blue-green pigment + fruity odor + oxidase positive + growth at 42°C.

Burkholderia pseudomallei

Lecture p. 3
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-negative obligate aerobic rod
  • Motile
  • Oxidase positive
  • Indole negative
  • Non-lactose fermenter
  • Grows at 42°C
  • Colistin and gentamicin resistant
  • Wright stain shows bipolar thickening
  • Blood, sputum, urine, throat swab, or aspirated pus
  • BAP: smooth creamy white at 24 h, then dried and wrinkled with purplish hue at 48–72 h
  • MacConkey: colorless non-lactose fermenter
  • API 20NE and PCR are in the lecture summary
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Environmental persistence and intracellular pathogenicity are key features
  • Classified in the lecture as a Category B bioterrorism agent
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Causes melioidosis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Blood, sputum, urine, throat swab, or aspirated pus
  • BAP: smooth creamy white at 24 h, then dried and wrinkled with purplish hue at 48–72 h
  • MacConkey: colorless non-lactose fermenter
  • API 20NE and PCR are in the lecture summary
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture options include ceftazidime, imipenem, meropenem, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin-clavulanate, TMP-SMX
  • Common resistance listed: penicillin, ampicillin, first and second generation cephalosporins, gentamicin, tobramycin

ORGANISM PROFILE

Acinetobacter baumannii

Lecture p. 4
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → gram-negative coccobacillus that may look like paired cocci.
    • Do not misclassify it as a true coccus.
  • Oxidase → negative and catalase → positive.
    • Useful against oxidase-positive Pseudomonas.
  • Temperature → grows at 44°C.
    • Lecture contrasts this with P. aeruginosa at 42°C.
  • MacConkey → colored/lactose-fermenting result in the lecture.
    • Also grows on sheep blood agar.
  • API 20 + PCR.
    • PCR can differentiate it from A. lwoffii.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsular polysaccharide
    • Anti-phagocytic. Also protects against desiccation, host defenses, and disinfectants → major reason it persists in hospitals.
  • Biofilm + fimbriae
    • Promote surface/device persistence.
  • Phospholipase + outer membrane
    • Contribute to host-cell injury and survival.
  • Antibiotic resistance
    • The lecture identifies resistance as a primary determinant of clinical outcome.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Nosocomial pneumonia, especially ventilator-associated pneumonia
  • Bloodstream infection
  • UTI, endocarditis, meningitis
  • Skin, soft-tissue, and bone infection
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Respiratory, blood, urine, or wound specimens as indicated
  • Culture plus oxidase-negative profile and temperature growth
  • API 20 and PCR are lecture methods
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment anchors: carbapenems, polymyxin, aminoglycosides
  • Strict healthcare infection-control measures are emphasized
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: ICU/ventilator + MDR nosocomial infection + oxidase negative coccobacillus + growth at 44°C.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Haemophilus influenzae

Lecture p. 5
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram stain → small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli with bipolar thickening.
    • Use with the fastidious growth pattern.
  • Oxidase → positive and catalase → positive.
    • Supports H. influenzae.
  • Growth requirement → requires X factor (hemin) + V factor (NAD).
    • Chocolate agar releases these factors.
  • Satellite phenomenon → growth around a streak of S. aureus on blood agar.
    • S. aureus lyses RBCs and supplies the required factors.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule in invasive Hib
    • Encapsulated strains are linked to severe invasive disease.
  • Requirement for X + V factors
    • Not a toxin, but a decisive biological feature that explains chocolate-agar growth and satellite phenomenon.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Meningitis
  • Epiglottitis
  • Otitis media
  • Pneumonia and bacteremia
  • Pericarditis and cellulitis are lecture associations
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Chocolate agar or satellitism demonstrates X and V factor requirement
  • Clinical specimen depends on syndrome, including CSF or respiratory samples
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment section includes syndrome-directed antibiotic therapy
  • Prevention: Hib vaccination is the key high-yield anchor
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Unvaccinated child with meningitis or respiratory infection + pleomorphic coccobacillus + X and V factor requirement + satellite growth.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Bordetella pertussis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Nasopharyngeal specimen is the relevant respiratory sample.
    • The lecture laboratory figure emphasizes targeted respiratory sampling.
  • Culture uses special Bordetella media in the lecture workup.
    • Because the organism is fastidious, ordinary culture logic is not sufficient.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • FHA + pertactin
    • Adhesion factors that help attach to respiratory epithelium.
  • Adenylate cyclase toxin
    • Reduces phagocytic activity and causes hemolysis of RBCs in the lecture.
  • Dermonecrotic/lethal toxin
    • Causes inflammation.
  • Pertussis toxin
    • Mediates colonization and the toxemic stages of disease.
  • Tracheal cytotoxin
    • Damages ciliated cells → impairs mucociliary clearance. Stimulates IL-1 release → fever. Inhibits DNA synthesis.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Pertussis progresses through catarrhal → paroxysmal → convalescent stages
  • Paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop is the classic clue
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Nasopharyngeal specimen or cough plate
  • Culture plus PCR or antigen-based methods
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture treatment uses macrolide therapy and supportive care
  • Prevention: DPT-containing vaccination and droplet precautions
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Classic staged cough syndrome + ciliary injury from TCT. Think special respiratory culture and vaccine history.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Legionella pneumophila

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Special culture → charcoal yeast extract/BCYE-type medium is the lecture anchor.
    • Ordinary respiratory culture may miss it.
  • Clinical-lab pairing → water/aerosol exposure + atypical pneumonia syndrome.
    • Use the environmental clue before choosing routine respiratory flora.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Survives in macrophages by creating a Legionella-containing vacuole and inhibiting effective phagolysosomal killing
  • Biofilm in water systems supports environmental persistence
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Legionnaires’ disease → atypical pneumonia with high fever, malaise, mild or nonproductive cough, neurologic symptoms, and patchy infiltrates
  • Pontiac fever → milder flu-like illness without pneumonia
Diagnostic confirmation
  • BCYE culture
  • IFA, ELISA, and PCR are lecture laboratory methods
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture management is directed at intracellular atypical pneumonia and supportive care
  • Water-system control is an important preventive theme
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Legionnaires’ disease → atypical pneumonia with high fever, malaise, mild or nonproductive cough, neurologic symptoms, and patchy infiltrates Pontiac fever → milder flu-like illness without pneumonia

ORGANISM PROFILE

Yersinia pestis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-negative facultative intracellular bacillus
  • Bipolar “safety-pin” staining
  • Capsule is prominent in young culture or animal tissue
  • Can grow at 27°C
  • Culture on MacConkey, plus anti-F1 serology and PCR
  • Culture, anti-F1 antibody serology, and PCR
  • Clinical epidemiology and vector exposure are major clues
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • F1 capsule
  • V and W antigens protect against intracellular killing
  • Yop proteins impair phagocytes
  • Pesticin, coagulase, and fibrinolysin are lecture virulence factors
  • Category A pathogen in the lecture
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Bubonic plague → lymph-node enlargement or buboes
  • Septicemic plague → DIC, purpura, acral ischemia and necrosis
  • Pneumonic plague → rapid respiratory failure, cyanosis, and septicemia
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Culture, anti-F1 antibody serology, and PCR
  • Clinical epidemiology and vector exposure are major clues
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture: streptomycin and chloramphenicol
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Flea/rodent exposure + bubo, hemorrhagic septicemia, or rapidly progressive pneumonic plague + safety-pin/bipolar-staining GNR + anti-F1/PCR.
GENERALITIES

How anaerobic infections announce themselves

Lecture p. 1–3

Why oxygen is toxic

Obligate anaerobes usually lack adequate SOD and catalase. They survive in low-redox sites such as the oropharynx, colon, deep skin appendages, devitalized tissue, ischemic tissue and abscesses.

Why infections are polymicrobial

Facultative anaerobes consume oxygen. The environment becomes more anaerobic and allows obligate anaerobes to multiply.

Clinical clueWhat it means in the lecture
Adjacent to mucosal surfaceThink endogenous mixed flora.
Foul-smelling dischargeShort-chain fatty acid metabolism is the lecture explanation.
Necrotic or gangrenous tissue with gasCO₂ or H₂ accumulation suggests anaerobic metabolism.
No growth on aerobic blood cultureRaises suspicion for anaerobic bacteremia or endocarditis.
Black exudatePigmented Prevotella or Porphyromonas.
Sulfur granulesClassic clue for Actinomyces in this lecture.
Must Know
Most endogenous anaerobic infections arise from the patient’s own normal flora after tissue disruption, ischemia, surgery, trauma, foreign bodies or malignancy.
Lecture summary: abscess formation is the usual manifestation of endogenous anaerobes.

CLOSTRIDIA

Four toxin syndromes you must separate

Lecture p. 9–13
OrganismToxin / mechanismClassic disease clueHigh-yield lab / management anchor
C. perfringensα-toxin = lecithinase / phospholipase C
Cell membrane destruction and myonecrosis		Gas gangrene with black necrotic tissue and gas
Food poisoning causes diarrhea and abdominal pain without fever or vomiting in the lecture		Double zone hemolysis on BAP
Nagler test demonstrates lecithinase
C. tetaniTetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter releaseSpastic paralysis
Trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus
Autonomic dysfunction is a major cause of death		Human tetanus immunoglobulin + toxoid
Wound care and metronidazole are lecture treatment anchors
C. botulinumBotulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → no ACh releaseDescending flaccid paralysis
Foodborne canned food, wound, infant honey, iatrogenic botulism		Adult antitoxin or infant human botulism immunoglobulin
Mechanical ventilation when needed
C. difficileTcdA enterotoxin and TcdB cytotoxinAntibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitisCCFA culture features
PCR for toxin B gene
Lecture calls cytotoxin tissue-culture detection the standard diagnostic method
Do Not Confuse
Tetanus = too much contraction because inhibitory neurotransmission is blocked.
Botulism = no contraction because acetylcholine release is blocked.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Peptostreptococcus

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-positive anaerobic coccus, spherical or ovoid
  • Pairs, tetrads, clumps, or chains
  • Capsulated, fastidious, slow-growing
  • Difficult to isolate
  • Gas-liquid chromatography metabolite: isocaproic acid
  • Deep aspirate or abscess material with anaerobic transport
  • Prolonged anaerobic culture
  • Biochemical identification or metabolite analysis
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Normal flora of colon, mouth, skin, and genitourinary tract
  • Anaerobic growth and polymicrobial synergy are major disease mechanisms
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Abscesses throughout CNS, head and neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, skin, bone, joints, and soft tissue
  • Usually polymicrobial
  • Can participate in generalized necrotizing soft-tissue infection
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Deep aspirate or abscess material with anaerobic transport
  • Prolonged anaerobic culture
  • Biochemical identification or metabolite analysis
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Use anaerobe-active therapy guided by site and susceptibility
  • Drainage and source control are important for abscess disease

Veillonella

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-negative anaerobic coccus
  • Oxidase negative
  • Catalase negative
  • Non-motile
  • Contains LPS
  • Normal flora of mouth and colon
  • Anaerobic culture and biochemical identification
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Uses lactate produced by oral streptococci and contributes to oral biofilm ecology
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Dental plaque and caries associations
  • Can cause osteomyelitis, pyelonephritis, meningitis, endocarditis, and hepatic abscess
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Anaerobic culture and biochemical identification
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Anaerobe-active therapy is guided by syndrome and susceptibility
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Dental plaque and caries associations Can cause osteomyelitis, pyelonephritis, meningitis, endocarditis, and hepatic abscess
ORGANISM PROFILE

Bacteroides fragilis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • BBE agar → growth despite bile.
    • B. fragilis is bile resistant.
  • Catalase → can be positive.
    • Lecture calls this out despite anaerobic status.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule is antiphagocytic and strongly linked to abscess formation
  • Fimbriae support adhesion
  • Enterotoxin can cause diarrhea
  • SOD helps oxygen tolerance
  • Lecture notes its LPS is less toxic than typical Gram-negative endotoxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Intra-abdominal infection and abscess after surgery, trauma, appendicitis, or diverticulitis
  • Bacteremia
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease and ovarian abscess
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Deep aspirate or sterile-site fluid with anaerobic transport
  • BBE agar and anaerobic culture
  • Biochemical identification after colony recovery
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture anaerobic GNR agents include metronidazole, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, and cefoxitin
  • Beta-lactamase-mediated resistance is an important clue
  • Drain abscesses and control source
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Intra-abdominal infection and abscess after surgery, trauma, appendicitis, or diverticulitis Bacteremia
ORGANISM PROFILE

Prevotella

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Culture pigment → brown or black pigment.
    • Pair with oral or genital anaerobic disease.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Capsule and immunoglobulin proteases are emphasized for pathogenicity
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Oral, head-and-neck, and genital polymicrobial anaerobic infections
  • Black-pigmented exudate is a diagnostic clue
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Anaerobic culture and pigment observation
  • Lecture anaerobe algorithm uses vancomycin resistance to support Prevotella among pigmented isolates
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Anaerobe-active treatment plus source control
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Oral, head-and-neck, and genital polymicrobial anaerobic infections Black-pigmented exudate is a diagnostic clue
ORGANISM PROFILE

Porphyromonas

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Culture pigment → brown or black pigment.
    • Pigmented anaerobe clue.
  • Gas-liquid chromatography → isobutyric acid.
    • Metabolic product used for speciation in the lecture.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Hemagglutinin and proteases are lecture virulence factors
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Oral and periodontal polymicrobial infection
  • May contribute to abscesses and invasive anaerobic disease
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Pigmented anaerobic culture
  • Lecture algorithm uses vancomycin sensitivity to separate it from Prevotella
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Anaerobe-active therapy and drainage when abscess is present
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Oral and periodontal polymicrobial infection May contribute to abscesses and invasive anaerobic disease
ORGANISM PROFILE

Fusobacterium necrophorum

Lecture p. 2
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Morphology → fusiform/spindle-shaped anaerobic gram-negative rod.
    • The shape itself is a major clue.
  • Biochemical tests may include indole, methyl red, and Voges-Proskauer.
    • The lecture notes aerobic/facultative biochemical tests can also be used.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • LPS, hemagglutinin, hemolysin, and platelet aggregation support thrombosis and dissemination
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Lemierre disease with internal-jugular thrombophlebitis after oropharyngeal infection
  • Can follow otitis, sinusitis, dental procedures, trauma, or mononucleosis
  • Septic embolic spread can involve lungs, liver, endocardium, and joints
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Anaerobic culture from appropriate sterile-site or aspirated material
  • Fusiform morphology and biochemical profile
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Anaerobe-active therapy plus urgent source control for deep infection
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Lemierre disease with internal-jugular thrombophlebitis after oropharyngeal infection Can follow otitis, sinusitis, dental procedures, trauma, or mononucleosis

Fusobacterium nucleatum

Lecture p. 2
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Gram-negative spindle-shaped or pointed anaerobic rod
  • Normal oral, gingival, genital, GI, and upper-respiratory flora
  • Metabolite clue: valeric acid
  • Blood agar may show breadcrumb colonies
  • UV fluorescence can be chartreuse yellow-green
  • Anaerobic culture plus morphology and fluorescence
  • Lecture algorithm notes phosphatase negativity
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Lectin-mediated attachment and LPS are lecture virulence features
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Periodontal disease
  • Can disseminate to endocardium and cause respiratory, brain, or liver abscesses and osteomyelitis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Anaerobic culture plus morphology and fluorescence
  • Lecture algorithm notes phosphatase negativity
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Anaerobe-active therapy with drainage or source control as indicated
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Periodontal disease Can disseminate to endocardium and cause respiratory, brain, or liver abscesses and osteomyelitis
ORGANISM PROFILE

Actinomyces species

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Microscopy → branching filamentous Gram-positive rods.
    • Unlike Nocardia, Actinomyces is not acid-fast.
  • Clinical specimen → sulfur granules in draining material.
    • A high-yield clue, although the lecture cautions other organisms may also produce sulfur granules.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Biofilm and local tissue invasion support chronic suppurative infection
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Cervicofacial actinomycosis or lumpy jaw after poor oral hygiene or dental procedures
  • Thoracic, abdominal, or pelvic actinomycosis after tissue disruption
  • IUD is a classic pelvic risk setting
  • Sulfur granules can appear in drainage
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Biopsy or aspirate with sulfur-granule examination
  • Gram stain, histopathology, fluorescence methods, and anaerobic culture
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Prolonged antibacterial treatment and source control are lecture management themes
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Cervicofacial actinomycosis or lumpy jaw after poor oral hygiene or dental procedures Thoracic, abdominal, or pelvic actinomycosis after tissue disruption

Cutibacterium acnes

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Formerly Propionibacterium acnes
  • Gram-positive anaerobic rod
  • Resident in deep hair follicles
  • Produces propionic acid as a metabolic clue
  • Common anaerobic contaminant in clinical specimens
  • Clinical lesion plus anaerobic culture when microbiologic confirmation is needed
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Sebum metabolism and follicular colonization promote inflammation
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Acne development in an occluded anaerobic follicle
  • Can be clinically relevant when recovered from deep or device-associated sites despite frequent contamination
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Clinical lesion plus anaerobic culture when microbiologic confirmation is needed
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Acne management is discussed in the lecture framework rather than a dedicated invasive-infection regimen
