ORGANISM PROFILE

Clostridium perfringens

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Blood agar → double zone of hemolysis.
    • Lecture attributes the zones to toxin activity.
  • Nagler test → positive lecithinase activity.
    • Egg-yolk lecithin is hydrolyzed by alpha toxin. Growth/toxin effect appears on the half without antitoxin because there is no neutralization.
  • Litmus milk → stormy clot reaction.
    • Lactose fermentation produces acid + gas while casein forms a clot.
  • Cooked meat broth → supports anaerobic growth before plating to BAP.
    • Use with tissue/gas-gangrene syndrome.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Alpha toxin
    • Major virulence factor with lecithinase/phospholipase C activity → lyses RBCs, fibroblasts, myocytes, platelets, and leukocytes → myonecrosis + hemolysis + tissue blackening.
  • Tissue pathogenesis
    • Toxin-mediated tissue injury + blocked blood supply → lower oxygen tension → CO₂/H₂ gas accumulation → gas gangrene.
  • Enterotoxin
    • Released with sporulation after contaminated food ingestion → diarrhea + abdominal pain, usually without fever or vomiting in the lecture.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Gas gangrene or clostridial myonecrosis with gas and tissue necrosis
  • Food poisoning with diarrhea and abdominal pain, generally without fever or vomiting
  • Hemolysis can be severe in systemic infection
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Deep tissue or wound specimen
  • Robertson cooked-meat broth followed by blood agar
  • Nagler and litmus-milk reactions are classic biochemical workup clues
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Urgent debridement or removal of necrotic tissue
  • Lecture options: high-dose penicillin G, clindamycin or metronidazole
  • Hyperbaric oxygen and antitoxin are also listed
  • Amputation may be required in severe disease
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Traumatic deep wound + rapid myonecrosis, gas, black tissue + double-zone hemolysis + positive Nagler/stormy clot.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Clostridium tetani

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Morphology → terminal spore with drum-stick appearance.
    • Classic exam morphology.
  • Culture → Robertson cooked meat broth then blood agar.
    • Lecture notes small flat translucent colonies with a narrow zone of hemolysis.
  • Diagnosis is strongly clinical.
    • The toxin syndrome is more important than relying on culture alone.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Tetanospasmin
    • Released after spores germinate in necrotic anaerobic tissue → travels along nerves to CNS → binds neuronal ganglioside/synaptobrevin-associated machinery → suppresses release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA + glycine → unopposed motor activity → sustained spastic contraction.
  • Tetanolysin
    • Helps local bacterial spread.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Wound exposure
    • Contaminated nail/soil inoculation into necrotic anaerobic tissue.
  • Motor pattern
    • Jaw spasm/lockjaw → trismus → risus sardonicus → generalized muscular rigidity and contractions with autonomic instability.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Primarily clinical syndrome with supportive anaerobic culture when performed
  • Small flat translucent colonies with narrow hemolysis are lecture culture clues
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Immediate human tetanus immunoglobulin plus tetanus toxoid
  • Wound care and control of spasms
  • Metronidazole is a lecture treatment anchor
  • Airway and ventilatory support when needed
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Dirty wound + lockjaw/risus sardonicus/spasticity. Mechanism is loss of GABA/glycine release.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Clostridium botulinum

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Spore → subterminal.
    • Pair with food, infant honey, wound, or iatrogenic exposure.
  • Culture → Robertson cooked meat broth then blood agar after anaerobic incubation.
    • Heat/alcohol treatment may be used to suppress other organisms before plating because spores are resistant.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Botulinum toxin
    • Toxin is endocytosed at the nerve terminal → light chain cleaves specific SNARE proteins → SNARE complex cannot form → synaptic vesicle cannot fuse with terminal membrane → no acetylcholine release → descending flaccid paralysis.
  • Clinical sequence
    • Eye-muscle weakness, ptosis, fixed/large pupils, diplopia → dysarthria/dysphagia → respiratory weakness.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Foodborne
    • Home-preserved/canned foods with low oxygen, high water content, and low acidity conditions.
  • Infant
    • Contaminated honey containing spores.
  • Neurologic pattern
    • Eye-muscle weakness → ptosis → large non-moving pupils → diplopia → trouble speaking/swallowing/breathing → descending flaccid paralysis.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Clinical neuroparalytic syndrome plus toxin and anaerobic laboratory testing
  • Culture can take several days
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Adult: lecture lists trivalent antitoxin
  • Infants: botulism immunoglobulin
  • Wound disease may use penicillin G
  • Mechanical ventilation and supportive care are critical
  • No honey for infants younger than 1 year and safe canning practices
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Home-canned food or infant honey + cranial weakness followed by descending flaccid paralysis. Mechanism is SNARE cleavage → no ACh release.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Clostridium difficile

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • CCFA → yellow colonies because C. difficile ferments fructose.
    • Lecture also notes horse-manure odor and yellow-green fluorescence under UV.
  • PCR → detects toxin B gene in stool.
    • A direct molecular clue.
  • Cytotoxin tissue-culture assay → cell change/lysis.
    • Lecture describes this as a standard diagnostic method and uses Vero cells.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • TcdA enterotoxin
    • Chemotactic for neutrophils → increases intestinal hemorrhage and fluid secretion → diarrhea.
  • TcdB cytotoxin
    • Inactivates Rho proteins → cytoskeletal/epithelial destruction → mucosal necrosis with inflammatory cells + fibrin → pseudomembranes.
  • Ecologic trigger
    • Prolonged antibiotics suppress competing normal flora → C. difficile overgrowth → toxin release.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Trigger
    • Prolonged antibiotics including clindamycin, ampicillin, beta-lactams, or fluoroquinolones in the lecture.
  • Disease
    • Diarrhea with pseudomembranous colitis. Colonoscopy can show whitish plaques/pseudomembranes.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Stool PCR for toxin B gene
  • CCFA culture
  • Cytotoxin detection in Vero-cell tissue culture is described as the standard in the lecture
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Stop or reassess the precipitating antibiotic when clinically appropriate
  • Use C. difficile-directed therapy according to the lecture and clinical severity
  • Infection-control and spore precautions are essential
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Recent antibiotics + diarrhea/pseudomembranes + CCFA yellow colonies or toxin-B PCR/cytotoxin assay.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Treponema pallidum

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Direct visualization → dark-field or immunofluorescence because the organism is too thin for routine visualization.
    • Silver impregnation can show organisms in tissue.
  • Culture → has not been continuously cultured on artificial media.
    • So serology is central.
  • Non-treponemal tests → reagin reacting with cardiolipin-based antigen.
    • Useful for screening and following activity in the lecture framework.
  • Treponemal tests → specific anti-T. pallidum antibodies.
    • Used for specific confirmation.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Outer-membrane proteins support adherence
  • Hyaluronidase promotes tissue invasion
  • Fibronectin helps prevent phagocytosis
  • Cardiolipin-associated reagin response forms the basis of nontreponemal testing
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Syphilis stages: primary hard chancre, secondary systemic disease including palms and soles rash, latent disease, and tertiary disease
  • Congenital syphilis is preventable with adequate maternal treatment
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Nontreponemal RPR or VDRL detect reagin against cardiolipin and are useful to follow treatment
  • Treponemal tests are more specific and may remain reactive for life
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Penicillin is treatment of choice
  • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can occur soon after therapy, especially in early syphilis
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Painless hard chancre → palms/soles secondary rash → latency/tertiary disease. Use non-treponemal + treponemal serology.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Borrelia species causing relapsing fever

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Irregular spirochetes about 10–30 µm long
  • Can be seen with Giemsa or Wright stain
  • Can be cultured in fluid media containing blood, serum, or tissue
  • Blood smear is most useful during the febrile stage when organisms are present
  • Exposure history and vector epidemiology support diagnosis
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Antigenic variation during one infection allows successive variants to escape the current antibody response
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Relapsing fever with 3–5 day febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals
  • Repeated cycles become progressively less severe
  • Headache, chills, and malaise are prominent during febrile periods
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Blood smear is most useful during the febrile stage when organisms are present
  • Exposure history and vector epidemiology support diagnosis
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture spirochete treatment uses penicillin or tetracycline-class therapy depending on organism and setting
  • Monitor for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Relapsing fever with 3–5 day febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals Repeated cycles become progressively less severe
ORGANISM PROFILE

Borrelia burgdorferi

Lecture p. 4
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Spirochete transmitted by Ixodes tick
  • Risk increases with prolonged tick attachment, especially 36–72 h
  • Classic erythema migrans in an exposed patient is a clinical diagnosis and serology is not required
  • Non-EM disease: two-tier serology → EIA or IFA then IgM/IgG Western blot if positive
  • PCR can be performed on a skin punch biopsy from lesion margin
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Tissue dissemination through lymphatics and blood
  • Immune-complex effects are discussed as contributors to some late manifestations
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Lyme disease with early erythema migrans followed by disseminated and late manifestations involving skin, musculoskeletal and other organs
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Classic erythema migrans in an exposed patient is a clinical diagnosis and serology is not required
  • Non-EM disease: two-tier serology → EIA or IFA then IgM/IgG Western blot if positive
  • PCR can be performed on a skin punch biopsy from lesion margin
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • The lecture supports treatment once the clinical diagnosis is established and does not require serology for classic EM
  • Prevention: minimize tick exposure and remove ticks promptly
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Lyme disease with early erythema migrans followed by disseminated and late manifestations involving skin, musculoskeletal and other organs
ORGANISM PROFILE

Leptospira interrogans / Leptospira

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Thin motile spirochete associated with animal reservoirs and contaminated urine, water, or soil
  • Swine are one important reservoir in the lecture
  • Exposure history plus leptospiral laboratory testing according to stage
  • The lecture emphasizes risk-stratified flood-exposure assessment
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Penetrates skin breaks or mucosal surfaces and disseminates hematogenously
  • Biphasic illness reflects bacteremic then immune phases
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Leptospirosis after flood or contaminated-water exposure
  • Fever, myalgia, headache and systemic disease
  • Severe Weil disease is a major complication
  • Aseptic meningitis may occur in the immune phase
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Exposure history plus leptospiral laboratory testing according to stage
  • The lecture emphasizes risk-stratified flood-exposure assessment
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Doxycycline is used for treatment or post-exposure prophylaxis in the lecture risk table
  • Prevention: avoid contaminated flood water, wear boots and gloves, rodent control, and protect food from animal contamination
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Leptospirosis after flood or contaminated-water exposure Fever, myalgia, headache and systemic disease
ORGANISM PROFILE

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Cell wall → absent.
    • Beta-lactam cell-wall inhibitors are ineffective.
  • Eaton agar → rich in cholesterol/nucleic acids, growth may take 2–4 weeks.
    • Colonies can be dome-shaped or fried-egg-like, though M. pneumoniae colonies may be smaller and less classic than M. hominis.
  • Chest X-ray → patchy infiltrate may appear despite relatively mild “walking pneumonia” symptoms.
    • This clinicoradiologic discrepancy is highlighted in the lecture.
  • Cold agglutinin test is a lecture diagnostic clue.
    • Use it as supportive rather than ordinary culture logic.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • P1 adhesin
    • Attachment organelle binds respiratory epithelial cells → prevents effective mucociliary clearance.
  • Lytic enzymes + superoxides + hydrogen peroxide
    • Released after attachment → epithelial injury + inflammation.
  • Inflammatory amplification
    • Replication damages respiratory epithelium and activates alveolar macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Walking pneumonia pattern
    • Respiratory symptoms may look relatively mild while chest X-ray shows a patchy infiltrate.
  • Extra-pulmonary
    • Encephalitis can follow atypical pneumonia in children with fever, mental-status change, and neck stiffness. Other lecture associations include erythema multiforme, neuritis, myocarditis, pericarditis, arthritis, and pancreatitis.
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Chest X-ray plus PCR
  • Eaton culture is slow and therefore not commonly used
  • Cold agglutinin testing is supportive only
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Beta-lactams are ineffective because there is no cell wall
  • Lecture options: tetracyclines, macrolides, fluoroquinolones
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Walking pneumonia + patchy CXR infiltrate + no cell wall + Eaton/cold-agglutinin clues.
ORGANISM PROFILE

Mycoplasma hominis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • No cell wall
  • Facultative anaerobe
  • Produces a classic fried-egg or dome-shaped colony more clearly than M. pneumoniae
  • Can be cultured from asymptomatic genitourinary colonization
  • Culture from the clinically involved site and Mycoplasma identification
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Lecture emphasizes colonization plus ascending genital and urinary infection rather than a named toxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Pyelonephritis
  • Salpingitis and tubo-ovarian abscess → PID
  • Post-abortal and postpartum fever
  • Can be isolated from joint fluid in disseminated infection
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Culture from the clinically involved site and Mycoplasma identification
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Cell-wall-active beta-lactams are ineffective for Mycoplasma
  • Use non-beta-lactam antimicrobial therapy according to lecture and susceptibility
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Pyelonephritis Salpingitis and tubo-ovarian abscess → PID
ORGANISM PROFILE

Ureaplasma urealyticum

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Extremely small free-living bacterium without a cell wall
  • Requires urea for growth
  • Urease positive → urea to ammonia and CO₂
  • Primarily genitourinary transmission
  • Urogenital specimen with Ureaplasma-specific culture or molecular testing according to lecture methods
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Urea metabolism is the key biochemical survival feature taught
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Non-gonococcal urethritis
  • Common vaginal or perineal colonizer
  • Associated with lung disease in premature low-birth-weight infants acquired during birth
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Urogenital specimen with Ureaplasma-specific culture or molecular testing according to lecture methods
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Beta-lactams are ineffective because the organism has no cell wall
  • Use non-cell-wall-active therapy according to clinical setting
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Use the organism’s morphology/test pattern first, then match the host setting and disease pattern. Non-gonococcal urethritis Common vaginal or perineal colonizer

Mycoplasma genitalium

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Cell-wall-deficient Mycoplasma of the genitourinary tract
  • Molecular testing is the practical organism-specific approach within the Mycoplasma framework
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Lecture emphasizes persistent genital-tract infection rather than a dedicated toxin
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Acute and chronic non-gonococcal urethritis in men
  • Cervicitis, endometritis, salpingitis, and infertility in women
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Molecular testing is the practical organism-specific approach within the Mycoplasma framework
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Beta-lactams are ineffective because Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall
  • Treatment uses non-beta-lactam agents according to the lecture

ORGANISM PROFILE

Chlamydia trachomatis

Lecture p. 11
Identification & biochemical test results
  • NAAT → major diagnostic method for genital infection.
    • Because Chlamydia is obligate intracellular, routine bacterial culture logic is not appropriate.
  • Developmental cycle.
    • Elementary body = infectious form. Reticulate body = intracellular replicating form.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Intracellular developmental cycle allows replication within epithelial cells
  • Group-specific LPS antigen is shared by Chlamydia
Disease & symptom pattern
  • A–C → trachoma
  • D–K → urethritis, cervicitis, PID, inclusion conjunctivitis, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia
  • L1–L3 → lymphogranuloma venereum
Diagnostic confirmation
  • NAAT from first-void urine or vaginal, cervical, or urethral swab
  • Direct fluorescent antibody for some extragenital specimens
  • Giemsa, Lugol iodine, EIA, and McCoy cell culture are lecture methods
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • STD: doxycycline or azithromycin
  • Neonatal pneumonia: oral erythromycin or azithromycin
  • Neonatal conjunctivitis: oral erythromycin
  • LGV: doxycycline or erythromycin for 21 days
  • No vaccine
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Genital disease or neonatal conjunctivitis/pneumonia + NAAT. EB is infectious and RB replicates.

Chlamydia pneumoniae

Lecture p. 11
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Obligate intracellular Chlamydia
  • Round dense inclusions
  • No glycogen in inclusions and iodine negative
  • One serovar
  • Human reservoir with aerosol person-to-person spread
  • Serology may be used, though interpretation is limited by prevalent antibodies
  • Molecular and Chlamydia-specific methods are preferred when available
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Intracellular epithelial infection is the central mechanism
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Upper and lower respiratory infection
  • Bronchitis and atypical pneumonia
  • Otitis media and sinusitis can occur
  • Lecture also notes an association with atherosclerotic vascular disease
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Serology may be used, though interpretation is limited by prevalent antibodies
  • Molecular and Chlamydia-specific methods are preferred when available
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture options: doxycycline, tetracyclines, macrolides, azithromycin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin for 10–14 days

Chlamydia psittaci

Lecture p. 11
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Obligate intracellular Chlamydia
  • Large variable dense inclusions
  • No glycogen and iodine negative
  • Bird reservoir
  • Transmission by inhalation of dried infected bird feces
  • Serologic testing may be used
  • Giemsa, immunofluorescence, and nucleic-acid methods are lecture diagnostic tools
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Intracellular replication after aerosol exposure
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Psittacosis with influenza-like illness or atypical pneumonia
  • Can be associated with pericarditis, jaundice or hepatomegaly, transverse myelitis, or encephalitis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Serologic testing may be used
  • Giemsa, immunofluorescence, and nucleic-acid methods are lecture diagnostic tools
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Preferred: doxycycline or tetracycline
  • Alternatives: macrolides or fluoroquinolone
  • Prevention includes control of infected bird exposure

ORGANISM PROFILE

Rickettsia rickettsii

Lecture p. 12
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Special stains → Giemsa bluish-purple, Gimenez red on bluish-green background, Macchiavello bright red on blue.
    • Rickettsiae stain weakly with routine Gram stain.
  • Serology → IFA/ELISA is a major confirmation method.
    • Serologic evidence may not appear until the second week, so treatment of severe suspected disease should not wait.
  • Direct immunofluorescence can detect R. rickettsii in skin biopsy.
    • Real-time PCR can diagnose before serologic response.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • OmpA/OmpB
    • Mediate endothelial-cell adherence.
  • Endothelial replication + cell lysis
    • Organisms multiply in vascular endothelium → cell injury/lysis → vasculitis → increased permeability → rash, edema, and hemorrhage.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  • Fever, headache, and myalgia followed by rash that starts on extremities and can involve palms and soles
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Treat on clinical suspicion while confirmatory serology develops
  • IFA or ELISA and PCR are high-yield tests
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Doxycycline is the primary treatment anchor
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Tick exposure + rash/vascular leak picture. Endothelial vasculitis is the mechanism. Serology may lag, so severe suspected disease is treated clinically.

Coxiella burnetii

Lecture p. 14
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Serology / indirect immunofluorescence → preferred over culture.
    • Culture is not routine.

CORE IDENTITY

Why mycobacteria are acid-fast

Lecture p. 1
Mycolic acidsLong-chain, lipid-rich wall
→
Waxy impermeable cell envelope
→
Acid-fastnessCarbolfuchsin retained despite acid-alcohol
FeatureLecture anchor
MorphologyAerobic, non-spore-forming, non-motile bacilli
Growth~18 h doubling time. Culture may take 3–8 weeks.
StainZiehl-Neelsen → red bacilli against blue background.
Auramine-rhodamine → yellow-orange fluorescence.
CultureMiddlebrook 7H10/7H11, Löwenstein-Jensen, and Middlebrook 7H9/MGIT are lecture-listed media.
Clinical Pearl
Obligate aerobe + high PO₂ at the lung apex → the lecture links reactivation TB to apical cavitation.
TB PATHOGENESIS

From inhalation to granuloma

Lecture p. 3–5
Inhalation
→
Macrophage uptake
→
Intracellular survivalBlocks phagosome–lysosome fusion
→
TH1 responseIFN-γ activates macrophages
→
Granuloma + caseous necrosis
Must Know
Outcome can be containment / latent infection, progressive primary disease, or later reactivation when immunity wanes.
Caseous necrosis is the hallmark of the tuberculous granuloma in the lecture.
PRIMARY VS SECONDARY

Location and lesion pattern

Lecture p. 5
FeaturePrimary TBSecondary / Reactivation TB
SettingFirst exposure, often childhoodReactivation when immunity wanes
Typical siteMid / lower lung zones in lectureApical / upper-lobe preference
Classic lesionGhon focus + hilar lymph node involvement = Ghon complexCavitary destructive disease pattern
Potential outcomeFibrosis and calcification can produce a calcified / Ranke complexMore symptomatic pulmonary disease and transmission risk
Clinical Cue
Classic TB triad emphasized in lecture: fever + night sweats + weight loss.
Pulmonary clue: chronic productive cough > 2–3 weeks.
TB DIAGNOSIS

What each test tells you

Lecture p. 5–6
TestHigh-yield interpretation from lecture
PPD / MantouxDelayed hypersensitivity read at 48–72 h. Measure induration, not erythema.
5–10–15 rule5 mm high-risk patients such as HIV or recent close contact.
10 mm increased-risk groups.
≥15 mm low-risk group.
IGRAImmune-based evidence of TB infection.
AFB smearRapid screening for acid-fast bacilli.
NAATRapid molecular detection and key role in modern diagnosis.
CultureAbsolute gold standard for proving active disease in the lecture by isolating tubercle bacillus.
Exam Trap
A positive PPD or IGRA does not prove active TB disease.
Severe immunosuppression can produce a false-negative PPD.
TB TREATMENT

RIPE at a glance

Lecture p. 7
DrugLecture mechanism / adverse-effect anchor
RifampinInhibits RNA polymerase. Lecture notes body-fluid discoloration and drug-interaction concerns.
IsoniazidInhibits mycolic-acid synthesis. Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine B6 when neuropathy risk is present.
PyrazinamideActive in acidic intracellular environment. Hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia are lecture anchors.
EthambutolInhibits arabinogalactan synthesis. Optic neuritis with red-green color-vision loss.
Program anchor
The lecture emphasizes DOT / DOTS to support adherence, completion, reduced transmission and reduced drug resistance.
NTM + LEPROSY

High-yield non-tuberculous mycobacteria

Lecture p. 8–12
OrganismHigh-yield lecture clue
MACImportant opportunistic pathogen in HIV / AIDS. Lecture emphasizes disseminated disease at very low CD4 counts and chronic pulmonary disease in older adults with bronchiectasis.
M. kansasiiPulmonary NTM disease pattern that can mimic TB.
M. ulceransChronic destructive skin lesion pattern.
M. lepraeLeprosy with tuberculoid vs lepromatous spectrum. Clinical exam and skin biopsy with acid-fast staining are lecture diagnostic anchors.
M. marinumSkin infection after aquatic exposure / minor trauma pattern.

ORGANISM PROFILE

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Ziehl-Neelsen → red acid-fast bacilli against a blue background.
    • Mycolic-acid-rich wall retains carbolfuchsin despite acid-alcohol.
  • Fluorochrome auramine-rhodamine → yellow-orange fluorescence.
    • Lecture notes higher sensitivity, though it is not the Philippines preference cited in the lecture.
  • Culture → Löwenstein-Jensen takes weeks. Middlebrook media and MGIT are also used.
    • Lecture framing: staining is a screening tool while culture confirms/speciates.
  • TST / PPD → read induration at 48–72 h.
    • Interpretation uses the lecture’s 5–10–15 mm risk-based rule.
  • IGRA → immune-response test for infection.
    • Like TST, it does not by itself prove active TB disease.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Cord factor / TDM
    • Toxic glycolipid responsible for serpentine cord growth and described as a major virulence property.
  • Sulfatide-like surface defense described in the lecture
    • Inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion → permits survival and proliferation within macrophages.
  • Mycolic-acid-rich wall
    • Supports acid-fastness, environmental resistance, and chronic persistence.
  • Cell-wall lipids + host delayed hypersensitivity
    • Drive granuloma formation and caseous tissue injury rather than a classic secreted exotoxin syndrome.
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Primary pulmonary TB → Ghon focus and Ghon complex
  • Latent infection can reactivate
  • Reactivation TB classically cavitates in upper lobes
  • Can disseminate to miliary and extrapulmonary TB
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Sputum AFB smear for screening
  • Culture for confirmation and species identification
  • Molecular rapid tests such as GeneXpert or Truenat are lecture anchors
  • TST or PPD and IGRA indicate infection, not necessarily active disease
  • Chest imaging supports active-disease evaluation
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Active TB: RIPE = rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
  • Minimum treatment is 6 months in the lecture
  • DOT supports adherence
  • Give pyridoxine with isoniazid in patients at neuropathy risk
  • Prevention includes prompt treatment, contact tracing, ventilation, respirators, and BCG for severe childhood TB protection
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Chronic TB syndrome + acid-fast bacilli + slow culture. Reactivation classically favors the oxygen-rich apex with cavitation.

Lecture p. 2
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Member of the M. tuberculosis complex
  • Acid-fast mycobacterium
  • Humans can acquire infection by inhalation or ingestion of unpasteurized milk
  • Mycobacterial culture and species identification within the TB-complex framework
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Pathogenicity resembles M. tuberculosis. Route of entry determines lesion pattern
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Inhalation → pulmonary lesions
  • Ingestion of unpasteurized milk → gastrointestinal lesions
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Mycobacterial culture and species identification within the TB-complex framework
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Treatment follows TB-complex principles
  • Prevention: pasteurization of milk
  • Live attenuated M. bovis is the basis of BCG vaccine

ORGANISM PROFILE

Mycobacterium avium complex (M. avium, M. chimaera, M. intracellulare)

Lecture p. 8
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Most common NTM group in the lecture
  • Non-motile, aerobic, slow-growing
  • Lowenstein-Jensen growth in 10–21 days
  • Forms smooth non-pigmented colonies
  • Environmental water, soil, birds, plumbing and biofilms
  • Not spread person-to-person in the lecture
  • Symptoms can resemble TB but diagnosis is confirmed by culture and species identification
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Surface glycopeptidolipids protect against lysosomal enzymes and support survival inside macrophages
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Advanced AIDS → disseminated disease, especially at very low CD4 counts
  • Chronic pulmonary disease in older adults with bronchiectasis
  • Lady Windermere pattern
  • Pediatric cervical lymphadenitis
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Symptoms can resemble TB but diagnosis is confirmed by culture and species identification
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Pulmonary or disseminated MAC: macrolide + ethambutol + rifamycin
  • Severe disease may add IV aminoglycoside
  • Refractory or macrolide-resistant disease may add inhaled amikacin or clofazimine
  • Continue pulmonary therapy 12 months after negative sputum cultures
  • MAC lymphadenitis → surgical excision
  • AIDS CD4 <50 → macrolide prophylaxis in the lecture

Mycobacterium ulcerans

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Fastidious, extremely slow-growing NTM
  • Prefers cooler temperature around 30°C
  • Associated with tropical wetlands
  • Transmission linked to mosquito or aquatic-insect bites
  • Not person-to-person in the lecture
  • Clinical pattern plus mycobacterial identification from lesion material

  • Lecture-supported toxin concept
    • The lecture states that organisms can release toxins that cause massive tissue death, producing enlarging necrotizing skin ulcers and severe soft-tissue edema. It does not name the toxin in this lecture, so this reviewer does not add an outside toxin name.

Diagnostic confirmation
  • Clinical pattern plus mycobacterial identification from lesion material
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lecture lists an 8-week antibiotic course for treatment
  • Early diagnosis is important before extensive tissue destruction

ORGANISM PROFILE

Mycobacterium leprae

Lecture p. 1
Identification & biochemical test results
  • Acid-fast stain → AFB-positive rods that may form clumps/globi.
    • Organism cannot be cultivated in vitro in routine media.
  • PCR → detects M. leprae DNA.
    • Useful direct identification method.
  • Lepromin skin test.
    • Induration after 48 h indicates cell-mediated response. Positive in tuberculoid, negative in lepromatous. It helps classify the type rather than simply diagnose infection.
Toxins / virulence → mechanism
  • Phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1) supports Schwann-cell invasion and immune evasion
  • Clinical spectrum reflects host cell-mediated immunity
Disease & symptom pattern
  • Leprosy or Hansen disease
  • Lepromatous form → many bacilli, diffuse disease, weak cell-mediated immunity
  • Tuberculoid form → few well-demarcated anesthetic lesions, granulomas, strong Th1 response and asymmetric nerve involvement
Diagnostic confirmation
  • Clinical exam, slit-skin smear, skin biopsy with acid-fast stain, and PCR
  • Lepromatous form: many AFB in foam cells
  • Tuberculoid form: few AFB with granulomas
  • Lepromin negative in lepromatous and positive in tuberculoid form
Treatment & prevention anchors
  • Lepromatous: dapsone + rifampin + clofazimine for 12 months
  • Tuberculoid: dapsone + rifampin for 6 months
  • Prevention: contact tracing, early MDT, single-dose rifampicin PEP for contacts, BCG cross-protection
Case-stem shortcutIf you see: Cool-site skin/nerve disease + AFB in tissue. Lepromin positive favors tuberculoid, negative favors lepromatous.

APPLICATION / CASE SCENARIOS

Disease-first differential page

Same disease → different bacteria
How to answer a vignette
Do not start by memorizing the whole disease list. Start with the syndrome, then use the host/exposure, then the most decisive laboratory result. The last step is explaining the toxin or virulence mechanism when the question asks “why.”
1. Name the syndromePneumonia, meningitis, UTI, diarrhea, wound, STI, paralysis
→
2. Use host/exposureAge, pregnancy, asplenia, ventilator, catheter, animal, water, food, vector
→
3. Match morphologyGram pattern, shape, spores, acid-fastness, intracellular biology
→
4. Pick the decisive testCulture color, enzyme test, special medium, NAAT, serology
→
5. Explain the mechanismCapsule, toxin, adhesin, enzyme, intracellular strategy
CASE DIFFERENTIAL

Pneumonia & respiratory syndromes

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
Typical pneumoniaStreptococcus pneumoniae
  • Rust-colored sputum.
  • Asplenia or impaired splenic function is a major severe-disease clue.
  • Alpha hemolytic.
  • Optochin sensitive.
  • Bile soluble.
  • Encapsulated lancet diplococci.
Lobar / necrotizing pneumoniaKlebsiella pneumoniae
  • Alcohol use, diabetes, hospitalized/ventilated patient.
  • Sudden fever/chills, severe productive cough, currant-jelly sputum, pleurisy, dyspnea, cyanosis.
  • CXR may show abscesses/cavitation.
  • Large mucoid pink lactose-fermenting colonies on MAC.
  • Nonmotile.
  • IMViC --++.
  • TSI A/A + gas, no H₂S.
  • String test >5 mm if hypermucoviscous.
Ventilator / CF pneumoniaPseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Ventilator or respiratory equipment, cystic fibrosis, severe burn, immunocompromise.
  • Water/environmental exposure may coexist.
  • Non-lactose fermenter.
  • Blue-green pyocyanin.
  • Fruity odor.
  • Oxidase +.
  • Growth at 42°C.
  • Fluoresces under UV.
Ventilator / hospital pneumoniaAcinetobacter baumannii
  • Critically ill, prolonged hospitalization, ventilator exposure.
  • Often multidrug resistant.
  • Gram-negative coccobacillus, may look like paired cocci.
  • Oxidase −, catalase +.
  • Growth at 44°C.
  • API 20 / PCR.
Respiratory infection / pediatric invasive diseaseHaemophilus influenzae
  • Upper/lower respiratory disease.
  • Unvaccinated child raises concern for invasive Hib disease.
  • Pleomorphic GNR/coccobacillus.
  • X + V factor requirement.
  • Chocolate agar.
  • Satellite growth around S. aureus on BAP.
  • Oxidase +, catalase +.
Atypical / walking pneumoniaMycoplasma pneumoniae
  • Relatively mild “walking” symptoms but patchy infiltrates on CXR.
  • May have extra-pulmonary neurologic or inflammatory manifestations.
  • No cell wall.
  • Eaton agar slow growth.
  • Cold-agglutinin clue.
Legionnaires diseaseLegionella pneumophila
  • Water/aerosol source such as cooling systems.
  • Pneumonia with fever, cough, headache in the lecture outbreak description.
  • Requires special charcoal yeast extract/BCYE-type culture rather than ordinary media.
Q-fever atypical pneumoniaCoxiella burnetii
  • Goat/sheep/cattle exposure.
  • Inhaled contaminated dust/aerosol, not an arthropod bite.
  • Acute disease can resemble influenza, atypical pneumonia, or hepatitis.
  • Serology/IFA rather than routine culture.
Reactivation pulmonary TBMycobacterium tuberculosis
  • Chronic infection pattern.
  • Reactivation classically favors the apex and can cavitate because of high oxygen tension.
  • Acid-fast stain.
  • Slow mycobacterial culture.
  • TST/IGRA indicate infection but do not alone prove active disease.
CASE DIFFERENTIAL

Meningitis & CNS infection

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
MeningitisStreptococcus pneumoniae
  • Encapsulated-organism risk, especially asplenia.
  • May coexist with pneumonia/otitis/sinusitis pattern.
  • Alpha hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble.
  • Blood/CSF culture.
Meningitis + meningococcemiaNeisseria meningitidis
  • Petechiae/purpura, shock, rapidly fulminant disease.
  • Complement C5–C9 deficiency or asplenia is a risk clue.
  • GND.
  • Oxidase +.
  • Glucose + maltose.
  • Capsule.
  • Blood + CSF.
Neonatal meningitisStreptococcus agalactiae
  • Neonate with sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis.
  • Maternal genital colonization.
  • Beta hemolytic.
  • Bacitracin resistant.
  • CAMP +, hippurate +.
Neonatal meningitisEscherichia coli
  • Neonate with invasive gram-negative infection.
  • Lactose +, EMB metallic sheen, indole +, motile.
Infant/child invasive meningitisHaemophilus influenzae type b
  • Unvaccinated child.
  • Can accompany respiratory-tract disease.
  • X + V factors.
  • Chocolate agar / satellite phenomenon.
Meningitis in vulnerable hostListeria monocytogenes
  • Pregnancy/newborn, elderly, or immunocompromised host.
  • Catalase +.
  • Tumbling motility at 25°C.
  • Narrow beta hemolysis.
  • Can grow in the cold.
Neonatal meningitis + brain abscessCitrobacter koseri
  • Newborn/premature infant <2 months.
  • Bulging fontanelle, seizures, rapid deterioration, brain abscesses are lecture clues.
  • C. koseri can be non-lactose fermenting.
  • Indole +, MR +, VP −, citrate +.
  • TSI K/A + gas, no H₂S.
Hypervirulent metastatic CNS infectionKlebsiella pneumoniae
  • Pyogenic liver abscess with metastatic spread can cause meningitis, even in otherwise healthy patients.
  • Hypermucoviscous mucoid phenotype.
  • String test >5 mm.
  • Nonmotile lactose fermenter.

Urinary tract infection

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
Cystitis / pyelonephritisEscherichia coli
  • Most common UTI pattern in the lecture.
  • P fimbriae / type 1 pili allow adherence despite urine flow.
  • Lactose + pink MAC.
  • EMB metallic sheen.
  • Indole +.
  • Motile.
UTI in young womanStaphylococcus saprophyticus
  • Classic demographic clue.
  • Catalase +, coagulase −.
  • Novobiocin resistant.
Catheter-associated / hospital UTIKlebsiella pneumoniae
  • Urinary catheter.
  • Dysuria, urgency, frequency, cloudy alkaline urine, pyelonephritis.
  • Mucoid lactose fermenter.
  • Nonmotile.
  • Urease weak/moderate +.
  • IMViC --++.
Stone-forming / catheter UTIProteus
  • Ascending UTI, catheter.
  • Very alkaline urine, struvite/carbonate-apatite stones.
  • Swarming motility.
  • Strong urease +.
  • H₂S +.
  • TSI K/A + H₂S.
Instrument/catheter UTIPseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Catheter, instruments, irrigating solutions.
  • Other Pseudomonas clues may be present.
  • Non-lactose fermenter.
  • Blue-green pigment.
  • Oxidase +.
  • Growth at 42°C.
Nosocomial UTIAcinetobacter baumannii
  • Hospital/ICU context, often MDR.
  • Oxidase −, catalase +.
  • Gram-negative coccobacillus.
  • Growth at 44°C.
Opportunistic UTICitrobacter
  • Hospital or compromised host.
  • Urinalysis may show nitrite + leukocyte esterase in the lecture.
  • Species-variable lactose/H₂S.
  • Citrate +, ONPG +.
  • Motile.
CASE DIFFERENTIAL

Diarrhea & gastroenteritis

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
Watery traveler’s diarrheaETEC
  • Acute watery, non-bloody diarrhea.
  • E. coli background: lactose +, indole +.
  • PCR detects lt + st.
Hemorrhagic colitis / HUSEHEC O157:H7
  • Bloody diarrhea.
  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome / acute renal failure risk.
  • SMAC: colorless/pale O157:H7.
  • Shiga toxin ELISA or stx1/stx2 PCR.
Bacillary dysenteryShigella
  • Fever, abdominal cramps, tenesmus, frequent small-volume bloody mucoid stool.
  • Nonmotile.
  • No H₂S.
  • TSI K/A, no gas, no H₂S.
  • ipaH PCR / Shiga toxin tests.
Salmonella gastroenteritisSalmonella
  • Foodborne gastroenteritis.
  • Non-lactose fermenter.
  • Motile.
  • H₂S + black-centered colonies.
CholeraVibrio cholerae
  • Profuse rice-water stool.
  • Rapid severe dehydration with tachycardia, hypotension, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes, thirst/cramps.
  • TCBS turns yellow from sucrose fermentation.
  • Oxidase +.
Food poisoning, preformed toxinStaphylococcus aureus
  • 1–8 h incubation.
  • Violent nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, rapid recovery, usually no fever.
  • Organism is catalase + and coagulase +.
  • Clinical timing strongly points to preformed heat-stable enterotoxin.
Emetic food poisoningBacillus cereus
  • Short incubation, classically rice/starchy foods, vomiting predominant.
  • Spore-forming Bacillus.
  • Emetic toxin is heat stable.
Diarrheal food poisoningBacillus cereus
  • Longer incubation, diarrheal syndrome.
  • Heat-labile diarrheal enterotoxin.
Food poisoningClostridium perfringens
  • Diarrhea + abdominal pain.
  • Lecture marks fever and vomiting as absent.
  • Anaerobic spore former.
  • Enterotoxin released with sporulation.
Antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitisClostridium difficile
  • Recent prolonged antibiotics.
  • Diarrhea + pseudomembranes.
  • CCFA yellow colonies, horse-manure odor, yellow-green UV fluorescence.
  • Toxin-B PCR or cytotoxin assay.
Seafood-associated gastroenteritisVibrio parahaemolyticus
  • Raw/undercooked seafood or water exposure.
  • “Meat-wash” watery stool in the lecture.
  • TCBS no yellow sucrose change.
  • TDH hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar = Kanagawa phenomenon.
Foodborne gastroenteritisCampylobacter jejuni
  • Undercooked/contaminated chicken is the high-yield exposure.
  • Curved/spiral motile GNR.
  • Microaerophilic growth and the lecture enzymatic profile.

Skin, soft tissue & wound infection

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
Abscess / purulent skin diseaseStaphylococcus aureus

Burn wound / ecthyma gangrenosumPseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Severe burn, bacteremia.

  • Human/animal bite or close animal exposure in the lecture.

  • Oropharyngeal source + invasive anaerobic disease.

Cervicofacial / pelvic actinomycosisActinomyces

  • Sulfur granules are a key clue.
  • Branching filamentous gram-positive, non-acid-fast anaerobe.
Seawater/seafood soft-tissue infectionVibrio vulnificus
  • Liver disease + seawater/seafood exposure.

Buruli ulcerMycobacterium ulcerans
  • Painless nodule → enlarging necrotizing ulcer + edema.
  • Tropical wetland/insect exposure.
  • Slow-growing mycobacterium preferring cooler temperatures around 30°C.

Disease / syndromeBacteriumCase clues & symptom patternHow to separate it in the lab
Subacute infective endocarditisViridans streptococci
  • Oral/dental source, damaged endocardium context.

  • Invasive S. aureus disease with bacteremia.

  • Use Bartonella exposure pattern from the lesson.

This is deliberately mechanism-heavy because tetanus vs botulism is a classic application contrast.

LAST-MINUTE RECALL

MCB bacteria cram sheet

Aerobic cocci

  • Catalase + = Staph. Catalase − = Strep.
  • Coagulase + = S. aureus.
  • Saprophyticus R and Epidermidis S to novobiocin.
  • Pneumococcus optochin sensitive. Viridans resistant.
  • Gonococcus uses glucose only. Meningococcus uses glucose + maltose and has capsule.

Enterobacteriaceae

  • All have O antigen.
  • Shigella + Klebsiella = no H antigen.
  • Shigella + Proteus = no K antigen.
  • E. coli = lactose +, indole +, EMB metallic sheen.
  • Salmonella = motile, H₂S +. Shigella = non-motile, H₂S −.
  • Proteus = swarming + urease.

Gram-positive rods

  • B. anthracis: pXO2 capsule, pXO1 PA/EF/LF, black eschar, Medusa head.
  • B. cereus: emetic 1–6 h, diarrheal 6–24 h.
  • Diphtheria toxin → EF-2 inhibition.
  • H. pylori → urease.
  • Cholera toxin → ↑ cAMP → water / electrolyte loss.

Non-enteric GNR

  • Pseudomonas: blue-green, fruity, oxidase +, 42°C, biofilm.
  • Pyocyanin blue-green. Pyoverdin fluorescent. Pyochelin siderophore.
  • B. cepacia → cystic fibrosis. B. pseudomallei → melioidosis.
  • Legionella → charcoal yeast extract. Legionnaires vs Pontiac fever.
  • Y. pestis → safety pin. Bubonic, septicemic, pneumonic plague.

Anaerobes

  • Foul smell + abscess + gas + mucosal source → anaerobes.
  • Black pigment → Prevotella / Porphyromonas. Sulfur granules → Actinomyces.
  • C. perfringens α-toxin = lecithinase.
  • Tetanus = spastic. Botulism = flaccid.
  • C. difficile = TcdA + TcdB → pseudomembranous colitis.

Spirochetes & atypicals

  • Syphilis: chancre → secondary rash → latent → tertiary.
  • Non-treponemal = reagin / cardiolipin. Treponemal = specific antibody.
  • Mycoplasma = no cell wall.
  • Chlamydia: EB infectious, RB replicates. Genital NAAT is test of choice.
  • Coxiella = Q fever via inhalation, no rash.
  • Rickettsial treatment anchor = doxycycline.

Mycobacteria

  • Mycolic-acid rich wall → acid-fast.
  • TB granuloma hallmark = caseous necrosis.
  • Primary: Ghon complex. Reactivation: apical cavitation.
  • PPD = induration, 48–72 h, 5–10–15 rule.
  • PPD / IGRA do not prove active TB. Culture is lecture gold standard.
  • RIPE. Ethambutol → optic neuritis. INH → B6 for neuropathy risk.
Final exam mindset
When a vignette gives a distinctive laboratory test, morphology, toxin mechanism, exposure, or syndrome, use that discriminator before the disease list.
The highest-yield pairs are the ones that look alike but split on one test: catalase, coagulase, novobiocin, optochin, lactose, motility, H₂S, urease, toxin mechanism, serologic target, or acid-fast behavior.
